title: Learning ragtime and Mule Face Blues
summary: His first rag was Twelfth Street Rag; he taught himself the hard King Oliver orchestration of Mule Face Blues.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Yes, I know you have. Can you tell me a little bit about ragtime style, where you first heard the, you might call the ragtime style, like maple leaf and those kind of rags?

Well, fact of the business, I've never heard maple leaf too good to re-reglect it now. I don't know so much about it, but the first rag that I ever remember learning were, were 12th Street rag. I was a youngster then, around eight, nine years old.
The solo you played quite often, the mule face blues. Where did you learn that?

Well, I learned that often in orchestration. That was a band number. Yeah. And we had it in several bands that I worked in. So, it was complicated for the majority of musicians to play it. Trumpet players. Yeah.

trombone players and everything, practically every band that get it was hard for them to play because it was kind of funny, you know, and every band that got a hold to it didn't care about fooling with it, you know. So I just took it up on myself to learn the whole thing by myself, you know. So some bands could play pretty good.
Yeah, Oliver made a record of it.

Well it's King Oliver's numbers, he wrote it, yeah. So well he had it kind of complicated for musicians at the time, of course today it wouldn't be too much from the play, it wouldn't be nothing because they're more experienced, you know, in the reading abilities anyway. So that's what made it hard. It took a pretty good reader, sight reader to read it, played good. So I'd taken it up on myself, I learned it off of the orchestration, you know.
